front: A battery's terminal voltage equals its emf only when {{c1::no current flows}}; under load $V = \varepsilon - Ir$.
why: Terminal voltage V = emf - Ir with internal resistance is a common circuit discrete

front: A cell membrane is about $7$ nm thick with $70$ mV across it. What field results, and why does it matter?
why: E = V/d applied to a membrane; the core relation is tested, this biological example is secondary

front: A charged capacitor is disconnected from its battery, then a dielectric is inserted. What happens to $V$ and $E$?
why: Dielectric inserted with capacitor isolated (Q fixed) is a frequently tested reasoning step

front: A charged rod attracts a neutral scrap of paper. What mechanism explains the attraction?
why: Polarization of a neutral object explains attraction; conceptual, rarely the point of a question

front: A dielectric is slid into a capacitor that remains connected to a battery. What happens to $V$, $C$, and $Q$?
why: Dielectric inserted with battery connected (V fixed) is a frequently tested reasoning step

front: A dielectric raises capacitance because its molecules polarize and create an internal field that {{c1::opposes}} the applied field.
why: Why dielectrics raise C (opposing internal field) supports the kappa card; second-tier mechanism

front: A gel is run at $100$ V instead of $50$ V across the same box. What changes?
why: Doubling gel voltage doubles drift speed and halves run time; applied electrophoresis reasoning

front: A parallel-plate capacitor has its plate separation doubled with charge held fixed. What happens to $C$ and $V$?
why: C = eps0 A/d with Q fixed, doubling d halves C and doubles V; standard capacitor proportionality

front: A passage reports an isolated droplet carrying $2.4 \times 10^{-19}$ C. Why is this measurement suspect?
why: Spotting a non-integer multiple of e is a common application, but the quantization card covers it

front: A proton and an electron are each released from rest in a uniform field. How does each move relative to potential?
why: Direction positive/negative charges move relative to potential is tested on nearly every exam

front: A pulse oximeter compares absorbance at {{c1::660 nm (red)}} and about $940$ nm (infrared), where the two forms of hemoglobin differ most.
why: Pulse oximeter wavelengths are trivia-grade detail far off the outline

front: A real image is one that:
why: Real vs virtual image (projectable) is a core optics distinction that shows up often

front: A static shock can involve thousands of volts yet be harmless because the transferred {{c1::charge and energy}} are tiny.
why: Why static shocks are harmless is illustrative trivia, not outline content

front: A surface ECG records potential differences of order {{c1::1 mV}}, produced by the heart acting as a large rotating electric dipole.
why: ECG signal magnitude and dipole model are off-outline detail

front: Because its phosphate backbone is negatively charged, DNA migrates toward the {{c1::anode}}, the positive electrode, during electrophoresis.
why: DNA migrating to the positive anode in electrophoresis is a classic biology-physics crossover

front: Between two protons the electrostatic repulsion exceeds the gravitational attraction by roughly a factor of {{c1::$10^{36}$}}.
why: The 10^36 electrostatic-to-gravity ratio is trivia

front: Bone appears white on a radiograph because calcium's high {{c1::atomic number}} makes it absorb X-rays far more strongly than soft tissue.
why: X-ray absorption vs atomic number is off-outline imaging detail

front: Capacitance depends only on {{c1::geometry and the dielectric}}, not on the charge stored or voltage applied.
why: Capacitance set by geometry and dielectric alone, not Q or V, is a frequently tested concept

front: Charge is quantized: every observed charge is an integer multiple of the {{c1::elementary charge}}, $e = 1.6 \times 10^{-19}$ C.
why: Charge quantization with e = 1.6e-19 C is foundational and used in calculations every year

front: Compare resistors in series and parallel.
why: Series vs parallel resistor combination rules are tested on essentially every exam

front: Define the electron volt and give its value in joules.
why: The electron volt definition and value is a commonly needed unit conversion

front: Describe the shape of the equipotential surfaces for a point charge and for a uniform field.
why: Equipotential surface shapes are useful context; rarely the tested point

front: Distinguish the units of electric potential from those of electric potential energy.
why: Distinguishing volts (J/C) from joules for PE is a common conceptual discrete

front: Electric potential is a {{c1::scalar}}, so contributions from several charges combine by algebraic addition.
why: Potential as a scalar that adds algebraically, unlike vector fields, is commonly tested

front: Energy stored in a capacitor is $U = {{c1::\frac12 CV^2}}$, equivalently $\frac12 QV$ or $Q^2/(2C)$.
why: U = 1/2 CV^2 and its equivalent forms are calculation equations tested every year

front: For two point charges the potential energy is $U = {{c1::kQq/r}}$, while a single charge sets up potential $V = kQ/r$.
why: U = kQq/r and V = kQ/r are core equations used in calculations on essentially every exam

front: Force on a charge moving in a magnetic field is:
why: F = qvB sin(theta) is the one magnetism equation tested every year

front: Give a case where the electric field is zero but the electric potential is not.
why: E = 0 but V nonzero inside a shell is a nice conceptual example but second-tier

front: Give Coulomb's law and Ohm's law.
why: Coulomb's law and Ohm's law are the foundational equations of the section

front: Give the electrical power formulas.
why: P = IV = I^2 R = V^2/R is used in calculations every year

front: Give the thin lens equation and magnification.
why: Thin lens equation and magnification are calculation equations tested every year

front: Grounding an object connects it to a charge reservoir, fixing its potential at {{c1::zero}}.
why: Grounding fixes potential at zero; supporting definition, rarely the tested point

front: How do capacitors combine?
why: Capacitor combination rules (opposite of resistors) are commonly tested

front: How do speed, frequency, and wavelength compare across the EM spectrum in vacuum?
why: c = f lambda across the EM spectrum is foundational and used in calculations every year

front: In a plane mirror, the image is:
why: Plane mirror image properties are a common optics discrete

front: In any isolated system the total electric charge is {{c1::conserved}}, even though it can be transferred between objects.
why: Conservation of charge is core but usually a background principle rather than the tested step

front: In electrostatic equilibrium, excess charge on an isolated conductor resides {{c1::entirely on the outer surface}}.
why: Excess charge on outer conductor surface is supporting conceptual detail

front: In gel electrophoresis, why do DNA fragments drift at constant speed instead of accelerating in the field?
why: Terminal drift velocity in a gel balances qE and drag; applied reasoning, second-tier

front: In vacuum every electromagnetic wave travels at $c = {{c1::3\times 10^8}}$ m/s; in a medium of index $n$ the speed drops to $c/n$.
why: c = 3e8 m/s and v = c/n are used in calculations on essentially every exam

front: Inserting a dielectric with constant $\kappa$ changes the capacitance to $C' = {{c1::\kappa C}}$.
why: C' = kappa C is a commonly tested capacitor relation

front: Kirchhoff's junction rule is based on conservation of:
why: Junction rule as conservation of charge is a common discrete

front: Kirchhoff's loop rule expresses conservation of:
why: Loop rule as conservation of energy is a common discrete

front: MRI uses radiofrequency photons. Why is it considered safer than CT?
why: MRI uses non-ionizing RF vs CT; plausible passage context, secondary

front: One coulomb is about {{c1::$6\times 10^{18}$}} elementary charges, which is why laboratory static charges are quoted in nC or $\mu$C.
why: Coulomb as 6e18 elementary charges restates the quantization card

front: Ordered by increasing frequency, the EM spectrum runs radio, microwave, infrared, {{c1::visible}}, ultraviolet, X-ray, gamma.
why: EM spectrum order by frequency is tested on nearly every exam

front: Photon energy is $E = hf = {{c1::hc/\lambda}}$, so shorter wavelength light carries more energy per photon.
why: E = hf = hc/lambda is a calculation equation tested every year

front: Resistors in SERIES have:
why: Series resistors card restates the series/parallel comparison card in this deck

front: State Snell's law and the condition for total internal reflection.
why: Snell's law and total internal reflection are tested on essentially every exam

front: The work done moving a charge along an equipotential surface is {{c1::zero}}.
why: Zero work along an equipotential is a commonly tested consequence of W = q delta V

front: The work required to move a charge $q$ through a potential difference $\Delta V$ is $W = {{c1::q\Delta V}}$.
why: W = q delta V is the core energy equation of electrostatics, used in calculations every year

front: Two identical conducting spheres carry $+8$ nC and $-2$ nC. They touch and separate. What charge does each carry?
why: Identical conductors sharing charge on contact is a classic frequently tested problem

front: Two parallel plates sit $2$ mm apart with $10$ V across them. What is the field between them?
why: E = V/d for parallel plates is a calculation used on essentially every exam

front: Two point charges of +2 μC and -4 μC are separated by 0.3 m. Is the force attractive or repulsive, and what is its magnitude? (k = $9 \times 10^{9}$ $N\cdot m^{2}/C^{2}$)
why: Coulomb's law calculation with sign reasoning; a common numeric discrete

front: What does conductive gel accomplish under an ECG electrode?
why: Conductive gel lowering contact resistance is off-outline clinical detail

front: What does the dielectric strength of an insulator determine?
why: Dielectric strength and breakdown is a useful definition but secondary

front: What is the field inside a conductor at electrostatic equilibrium?
why: Zero field inside a conductor at equilibrium is a commonly tested concept

front: What is the sign of the potential energy of two like charges versus two unlike charges?
why: Sign of U for like vs unlike charges is a common conceptual question

front: Where equipotential lines are drawn closer together, the electric field is {{c1::stronger}}.
why: Closer equipotentials mean stronger field is a commonly tested graphical inference

front: Which lens corrects myopia vs. hyperopia?
why: Diverging lens for myopia, converging for hyperopia is a common optics discrete

front: Which regions of the EM spectrum are ionizing, and what is the clinical consequence?
why: Which EM regions are ionizing is commonly tested and passage-relevant

front: Why are EEG signals harder to record cleanly than ECG signals?
why: EEG vs ECG signal size is off-outline clinical trivia

front: Why does a defibrillator discharge a capacitor rather than connect the patient directly to a battery?
why: Defibrillator as a capacitor discharge is a plausible passage application; secondary

front: Why does a grounded metal mesh around an MRI suite block outside radio signals?
why: Faraday cage around MRI restates the zero-field-inside-conductor card

front: Why is $60$ Hz household AC considered more hazardous than DC at the same voltage?
why: AC vs DC hazard by frequency is off-outline physiology trivia

front: Why is a bird perched on a single high-voltage line unharmed even at $10^5$ V?
why: Bird on a wire illustrates current needing a potential difference; conceptual example

front: Why is the same $120$ V outlet far more dangerous when your hands are wet?
why: Wet vs dry skin resistance applies Ohm's law; illustrative, secondary

front: Why must the electric field just outside a charged conductor be perpendicular to its surface?
why: Field perpendicular to a conductor surface is supporting electrostatics detail

front: X-rays and gamma rays overlap in energy and are distinguished mainly by their {{c1::origin}}.
why: X-ray vs gamma distinguished by origin is a plausible discrete but secondary
